$comment: Which samples in samples/workflows/ become recipe pages under docs/recipes/. `pnpm --filter @ai-orchestrator/docs gen:recipes` (run by the docs build and dev server) writes them. Fields: sample (file name); slug (page name; never rename a published slug, GitHub Pages cannot redirect); title (<= 54 characters, the page title adds ' | L2M'); description (<= 155 characters); keys (none | model | services: what it needs to run); keysNote (one short line, e.g. 'No API key'); time (optional, e.g. '5 minutes'); tags (lower case, the filters on /recipes/); whatYouGet (one sentence); summary (Markdown paragraph: what it does and when to use it); steps (optional Markdown strings, numbered after the download and import steps; replace the default 'run it as it is' steps); sections (optional [{ heading, body }] of hand-written Markdown after 'How it works': what a run really does, variants, limits); makeItYours and makeItSafer (Markdown lists, optional; safety controls are optional features, say so); related (glossary slugs); docs (further reading inside the docs).

recipes.title: Build an MCP agent with no API key in 5 minutes
recipes.description: Import a ready MCP agent that runs on a fresh L2M install with a built-in echo model and a mock MCP server, then swap in a real model and server.
recipes.whatYouGet: One agent with a chat model and two MCP tools, a clock and a calculator, that runs on a fresh install.
recipes.summary: A manual trigger starts one Agent Orchestrator node. Its chat model is the built-in echo provider, and its tools come from the mock MCP server that runs inside L2M: `get_current_time` and `calculator`. Nothing needs a key, a network connection or a separate server. Echo is not a real model: it repeats the prompt back and never asks for a tool, so a local run makes one model call and ends. That proves the wiring works. To see the agent call tools, attach a real chat model.
steps:
Click **Run** in the editor, or call the run API with your own question. The API takes an API key from **Settings › Account › API Keys**:

   ```bash
   curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/api/workflows/wf-mcp-agent-quickstart/execute \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $L2M_API_KEY" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"user_prompt": "What is 2340 * 0.17?"}'
   ```
Open the run in the execution history and click the **Agent** node to read its trace.
Then change one thing at a time (see below).

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body: We imported the file into a fresh install and ran it with the question above. The run succeeded in well under a second: - The **Agent** made one model call. The model was offered the two tools as `mock-mcp__get_current_time` and `mock-mcp__calculator`; L2M also adds a short note to the system prompt about its built-in `session_cache_list`, `session_cache_get` and `agent_clarify` tools. - Echo answered `Echo: What is 2340 * 0.17?`. The agent stopped after 1 iteration with `stopReason: "final_answer"`, and the **Output** node returned that text as `result`. - The two MCP Tool nodes are marked as used by the agent: they supplied the tool definitions. No tool ran, because echo asked for none. An empty question fails the run: the agent's user prompt template is `{{user_prompt}}`, and with nothing in it the Agent stops with "Agent Orchestrator user prompt is empty after template rendering".

sections.heading: See the loop with tool calls
sections.body: The demo's copy of this workflow plays an echo run too, so it shows no tool calls either. The demo's **Support agent** workflow plays a run recorded with a real model, in which the agent calls a knowledge-base tool once and a calculator tool twice before it answers: open it in the demo.

recipes.makeItYours:
- Replace the echo chat model node with a real one (OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint) on the agent's `chat_model` port. A model that supports tool calling can then call the clock and the calculator.
- Replace the mock MCP tools with a server from your [MCP server registry](/product/mcp-server-registry), such as a filesystem or database server.
- Write your own system prompt on the agent node, and raise `maxIterations` (4 in the sample) only if the task needs more steps.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- `calculator` has no read-only annotation, so L2M counts it as a write tool. Turn on the workflow's **No write tools** setting and it is blocked for the agent, while the clock stays. See [MCP tool policy](/product/mcp-tool-policy#no-write-tools).
- Require a person's approval before write tools run: see [human approval for agent tool calls](/guides/human-approval-for-agent-tool-calls).
- Cap model spend with a [budget](/product/budgets).

recipes.title: Webhook to AI agent with memory and MCP tools
recipes.description: Trigger an agent from a webhook, give it session memory and MCP tools, and secure the webhook with a bearer token or HMAC signature.
recipes.keysNote: A model: local Ollama or a provider key
recipes.whatYouGet: An agent behind a webhook URL, with per-session memory and two MCP tools, that any app can call with a question and a session id.
recipes.summary: A **Webhook Input** node at `POST /webhook/agent-demo` passes `system_prompt`, `user_prompt` and `session_id` from the request body to an Agent Orchestrator. The agent has a chat model, a **Simple Memory** node keyed by the session id, and two tools from the mock MCP server built into L2M. As shipped, the chat model points at a local Ollama server (`http://localhost:11434/v1`, model `qwen2.5:7b`), so you need that model, or you point the node at another one. As shipped, the webhook also has no authentication: secure it before you expose it.
steps: Open the chat model node and point it at a model you have: pull `qwen2.5:7b` into Ollama, type another model name, or switch the provider. Save.

Send a request:

   ```bash
   curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/webhook/agent-demo \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"system_prompt": "You are a helpful assistant.", "user_prompt": "What is 12 * 7?", "session_id": "demo-2"}'
   ```
Send a second request with the same `session_id` and a follow-up question. The agent now sees the first exchange.
Before anyone else can reach the URL, secure it (see below).

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body:
Two things are worth knowing before you call it from an app.

**A model error comes back as the answer.** If the chat model call fails (the model is not pulled, the server is down, the key is wrong), the agent does not fail the run. It returns the error message as its answer, such as `Provider ollama request failed (404): ...`, with `stopReason: "error"`, and the webhook replies with that text in `output.result`. If an app gets text like that back, open the run and look at the Agent node.

**Memory, checked with the echo model.** To test the webhook and memory without a model, we set the chat model to the built-in echo provider. Two requests with `session_id: "demo-2"` returned `Echo: What is 12 * 7?` and then `Echo: And what time is it in Toronto?`. The second run's agent messages held the first question and answer before the new question: that is the memory. Echo never calls tools, so this check says nothing about tool use; a model that supports tool calling can call `get_current_time` and `calculator`.

Memory keeps the last 20 messages of a session (`maxMessages`) and, with **Persist Tool Messages** off, leaves tool results out of it. The tools' connection names an HTTP endpoint (`http://127.0.0.1:7001/mcp`), but the `mock-mcp` server runs inside L2M: nothing has to listen on that port.

sections.heading: Secure the webhook
sections.body:
With no auth mode set, anyone who can reach your L2M can call the agent and spend your model budget. On the Webhook Input node:

- **Bearer token.** Set the auth mode to `bearer_token`, the auth header name to `authorization`, and pick a stored secret that holds the token. Callers then send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. We checked: without the header the call gets `401 {"error":"Unauthorized webhook request"}`; with it, the agent answers.
- **HMAC signature.** For callers that can sign requests, `hmac_sha256` checks a hex HMAC-SHA256 of `timestamp + "." + raw body`, sent with a timestamp header. Requests outside the replay window (300 seconds by default) and repeated signatures are rejected.
- **Idempotency.** Turn it on so a retried request with the same `Idempotency-Key` returns the first result instead of running the agent again; the same key with a different body gets `409`. Once it is on, every request must send the header, or it gets `400`.
- **Allowed addresses.** List the IPs or CIDR ranges that may call the trigger.

See [Secure webhooks](/security/secure-webhooks) for the signing format and error codes.

recipes.makeItYours:
- Switch the chat model to OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with its key stored as a [secret](/security/secrets).
- Replace the mock tools with a server from your [MCP server registry](/product/mcp-server-registry).
- Raise `maxMessages` on the memory node for longer conversations, or lower it to keep prompts small.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- The sample takes `system_prompt` from the request, so any caller can rewrite the agent's instructions. Write the system prompt on the agent node instead.
- Require approval before write tools: with **Ask before write tools** on, the agent pauses before `calculator` (it has no read-only annotation). See [human approval for agent tool calls](/guides/human-approval-for-agent-tool-calls).
- Cap what callers can spend with a workflow [budget](/product/budgets).

recipes.title: Supervisor and worker agents: a runnable example
recipes.description: A supervisor agent hands work to a researcher and a calculator worker, each with its own tools. Imports and runs with no API key.
recipes.whatYouGet: A Supervisor agent with two worker agents, each with its own chat model and MCP tools, that runs on a fresh install.
recipes.summary: A Supervisor node coordinates two worker agents. The researcher has an MCP knowledge-base lookup tool; the computer has a calculator and a clock. The Supervisor sees each worker as one tool and decides which to call for each step, and each worker runs its own agent loop. Every agent uses the built-in echo provider and the mock MCP server built into L2M, so it runs with no API key. Echo never asks for a tool, so a local run shows the wiring, not the delegation: the Supervisor answers on its first turn and hands nothing off. Attach a real chat model to see it delegate.
recipes.makeItYours:
- Give each worker its own real chat model on its `chat_model` port: a small, cheap model often does for a narrow worker, while the Supervisor needs one that plans well.
- Swap a worker's mock tools for your own MCP servers.
- Add a third worker on the Supervisor's `worker` port when a new kind of task appears, rather than giving one agent every tool. Each worker adds a tool to the Supervisor's list and model calls to each run, so add one only for a distinct job.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- Keep write tools on one worker only, and require approval for them: see [human approval for agent tool calls](/guides/human-approval-for-agent-tool-calls).
- Record a good run as a [golden run](/product/golden-runs) and replay it after each change.
steps: Click **Run** in the editor, or call the run API with a question for the team (as in the [zero-key agent recipe](/recipes/zero-key-mcp-agent), with the workflow id `wf-supervisor-worker-swarm`).
Open the run and click the **Supervisor** node to read its trace.
Then change one thing at a time (see below).

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body:
We ran the sample on a fresh install with "What is 17% of 2340, and what does MCP stand for?":

- The **Supervisor** made one model call and stopped after 1 iteration with `stopReason: "final_answer"`. Echo answered `Supervisor: What is 17% of 2340, and what does MCP stand for?`.
- Both workers, their chat models and their tools are marked **skipped** (`attachment_only_node`). Workers are not steps in the run: they run only when the Supervisor calls them, and echo never did.

The Supervisor is offered one tool per worker, named `delegate_to_` plus the worker's name with every character other than letters, digits, `_` and `-` turned into `_`: here `delegate_to_Worker__Researcher` and `delegate_to_Worker__Computer`. Each tool's description starts with "Delegate task to" and the worker's name, followed by the start of the worker's system prompt as a hint. Name workers so the Supervisor's model can tell them apart; two workers with the same name make the run fail.

sections.heading: See delegation in a recorded run
sections.body: The demo's **Research swarm** workflow is the same pattern with a researcher and an analyst, recorded with a real model. In its run the Supervisor calls `delegate_to_researcher`, then `delegate_to_analyst`, then writes the team summary: three iterations. Play it in the demo.

recipes.title: Serve an L2M workflow as an MCP tool
recipes.description: Turn a whole workflow into one MCP tool that agents and IDE clients can call, then serve it from a toolset with its own client token on the MCP gateway.
recipes.whatYouGet: A workflow that any MCP client can list and call as one tool, `answer_from_kb`, through L2M's MCP gateway.
recipes.summary: An **Expose as MCP Tool** trigger turns the workflow into a tool named `answer_from_kb`, with one required argument, `question`. Inside, an agent with the echo model and the mock `lookup_kb` tool answers it. Put the workflow in a toolset on the [MCP gateway](/product/mcp-gateway) and any MCP client holding a client token can list the tool and call it; each call runs the whole workflow. It runs with no API key. With echo, the answer is the question repeated back.
steps: In the sidebar, open **MCP → Toolsets**, create a toolset and add the workflow. Its endpoint is `/mcp/<slug>` (we named ours `kb-helper`).
Open **MCP → Clients**, create a client for that toolset and copy its token. It is shown once.
Call the tool with curl (below), or paste the client's configuration snippet into your MCP client.

sections.heading: Call it with curl
sections.body:
The gateway speaks MCP over Streamable HTTP. With the client token in `TOKEN` and the session id from step 1 in `SESSION`:

```bash
# 1. Open a session. The response carries an Mcp-Session-Id header.
curl -i http://localhost:4000/mcp/kb-helper \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-11-25","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1"}}}'

# 2. Call the tool in that session. (List them first with the same request and
#    "method":"tools/list", "params":{}.)
curl http://localhost:4000/mcp/kb-helper \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -H "Mcp-Session-Id: $SESSION" \
  -H "MCP-Protocol-Version: 2025-11-25" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"answer_from_kb","arguments":{"question":"What is MCP?"}}}'

# 3. End the session.
curl -X DELETE http://localhost:4000/mcp/kb-helper \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Mcp-Session-Id: $SESSION"
```

What came back on our install:

- `initialize`: HTTP 200 with an `mcp-session-id` header and `{"protocolVersion":"2025-11-25","capabilities":{"tools":{"listChanged":false}},"serverInfo":{"name":"l2m-kb-helper","title":"KB helper",...}}`.
- `tools/list`: one tool, `answer_from_kb`, with the description and input schema from the trigger.
- `tools/call`: `content` with the workflow output as JSON text, the same object as `structuredContent` (`{"result":"Echo: What is MCP?"}`), and the run's id in `_meta.executionId`.
- `DELETE`: `204 No Content`.

Each call is a full run, listed in the execution history with the trigger type `mcp_gateway`. The gateway speaks MCP protocol versions 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26. An MCP client library or app does these steps for you.

sections.heading: The sample's legacy routes are public
sections.body: The trigger also has a `path` (`kb-helper`) and `authMode: "public"`, which serve the older REST routes `GET /api/mcp-server/kb-helper/manifest` and `POST /api/mcp-server/kb-helper/invoke`. On our install both answered without any credentials, and `invoke` ran the workflow. They are not MCP, so MCP clients do not need them: set the trigger's auth mode to `bearer` with a stored secret, or remove the `path`, before you deploy. See [Expose a workflow as an MCP tool](/runtime/workflow-as-mcp-tool#legacy-rest-routes).

recipes.makeItYours:
- Change `toolName`, `toolDescription` and `inputSchema` on the trigger. The description is what other agents' models read to decide when to call your tool, so make it specific.
- Replace the agent's echo model with a real one, or replace the agent with a retrieval step and an LLM call, as in the [RAG knowledge base recipe](/recipes/rag-knowledge-base).
- Call it from another L2M instance: register `https://<l2m-host>/mcp/<slug>` there with the `http_mcp` adapter and the client token as a stored secret.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- Give each client only the toolsets it needs, the lowest role that works, and an expiry.
- Add [tool policy](/product/mcp-tool-policy) rules scoped to the client or the toolset, including require-approval rules.
- Cap each client with a [budget](/product/budgets) scoped to **MCP client** and a rate limit on the client.

recipes.title: RAG with a built-in knowledge base, no vector DB
recipes.description: Ingest documents into L2M's built-in knowledge base and answer questions from them, with no external vector database and no API key to start.
recipes.whatYouGet: A question-answering workflow that retrieves from a knowledge base stored in L2M's own database, with no vector database and no API key.
recipes.summary: A **Question** node holds the question. **RAG Retrieve** searches a built-in knowledge base for the three nearest chunks, a **Prompt Template** puts them into a grounded prompt, and an **LLM** node answers. The sample uses `token-embedder`, a hash-based demo embedder that needs no key (its search quality is poor), and the echo model. Echo returns the prompt it was given, which is useful here: the answer shows exactly what a real model would read. Swap both for real ones to get real answers.
steps: Create a knowledge base with the `token-embedder` and add a document, under **Knowledge** in the sidebar or with the API (below). Copy its id.
Open the **RAG Retrieve (KB)** node and replace `<your-kb-id>` with that id. Save.
Run it, then change the question on the **Question** node and run it again.

sections.heading: Create a knowledge base with the API
sections.body:
```bash
# Create a knowledge base (admin). The response holds its id: kb_...
curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/api/knowledge-bases \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $L2M_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "Helpdesk FAQ", "embedderId": "token-embedder", "embedderConfig": {}}'

# Load, chunk, embed and store a Markdown file in one call.
curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/api/knowledge-bases/$KB_ID/upload \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $L2M_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"filename": "helpdesk-faq.md", "sourceId": "helpdesk-faq-v1",
       "content": "# Helpdesk FAQ\n\n## Reset your password\nTo reset your password, open the sign-in page, choose Forgot password, and enter your work email. The reset link is valid for 30 minutes.\n\n## Change your billing plan\nAdmins can change the billing plan under Settings, then Billing. Changes apply from the next invoice.\n\n## Export your data\nGo to Settings, then Data, and choose Export. You get a ZIP file with one CSV per table.",
       "chunking": {"strategy": "recursive", "chunkSize": 300, "chunkOverlap": 0}}'
```

On our install the upload answered `{"sourceId":"helpdesk-faq-v1","documentsLoaded":1,"chunksInserted":2,"dimensions":64}`. The embedder you create the knowledge base with must match the `embedderId` on the RAG Retrieve node, or the question and the chunks are not compared in the same space.

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body:
We ran the sample on a fresh install, against a knowledge base holding a short helpdesk FAQ (a password-reset section, a billing section and a data-export section, stored as 2 chunks):

- **RAG Retrieve** returned both chunks, the password-reset chunk first (similarity 0.375, against 0.131 for the other), each with its `chunkId`, `sourceId` and score.
- **Grounded Prompt** numbered them `[1]` and `[2]` under "Context:" and added the question.
- **LLM** (echo) returned that whole prompt, prefixed with `Echo: `, and **Output** returned it as `result`.

Two things to know:

- **A missing id fails quietly.** Run the sample without replacing `<your-kb-id>` and it still succeeds: retrieval returns no documents and the prompt's context is empty. If answers look ungrounded, check the retrieve node's `documents` first.
- **The template asks for chunk ids, but the context shows numbers.** The prompt says "Cite the chunkId for every claim" while the context lists `[1]`, `[2]`. For citations that resolve to their sources, use the `citationInstructions` the retrieve node emits and the citation tools in [Knowledge bases](/nodes/knowledge-bases#citations-phase-9-4).

sections.heading: Variant: retrieve from a connector
sections.body: [`rag-flow.json`](https://github.com/TensorGreed/ai-orchestrator/blob/main/samples/workflows/rag-flow.json) loads documents from a **Connector Source** (Google Drive) on every run and retrieves from them in memory, with no knowledge base. As shipped it calls a local Ollama model (`llama3.1`). We ran it with the echo model and no Google credentials: the connector ran in demo-fallback mode and returned five built-in sample documents, and retrieval put the three closest to "How does MCP fit into an AI workflow builder?" into the prompt. Use a knowledge base when the documents should be ingested once and kept; use a connector for small sets that change between runs.

recipes.makeItYours:
- Use a real embedder (for example `openai-embedder`, with its key as a [secret](/security/secrets)) for the knowledge base and the same `embedderId` on the node. A knowledge base keeps the vector size of its first chunks, so start a new one when you change embedders.
- Replace the echo model with a real one on the **LLM** node.
- Set `searchMode` to `hybrid` to add keyword (BM25) matches to vector search, and add a **Rerank** node for better ordering. See [hybrid search](/nodes/knowledge-bases#hybrid-search-phase-9-3).
recipes.makeItSafer:
- Retrieved documents are outside content: a document can carry instructions for the model. [Content rules](/product/content-rules#outside-content-at-the-model-boundary) can check each retrieved document before it reaches the model.
- Cap model spend with a [budget](/product/budgets) once you switch to a paid model.
